Subsequently, the Lam lab and collaborators incorporated PacBio long-read sequencing, optical maps and DNA FISH to correct chromosome-level misassemblies in the initial reference, and establishing the second reference genome for S. polyrhiza (Hoang et al. 2018). With support from this award, we published the first long-read genome sequence of a Wolffia species, along with a transcriptomic analysis revealing a reduction in time-of-day dependent gene regulation in duckweeds (Michael et al. 2021). Wolffia species are the most morphologically reduced and fastest growing members of Lemnaceae, and make the world’s smallest flowers. Broadening the scope of duckweed genome references, the Martienssen lab and collaborators next produced eight chromosome- resolved reference quality assemblies of W. australiana, L. gibba, L. minor, L. turionifera, and three allotriploid hybrid L. japonica (L. minor x L. turionifera) clones, using Oxford Nanopore long reads and Hi-C contact maps (Ernst et al. 2025). Comparisons of the chromosome-scale assemblies demonstrated a high degree of synteny across all 21 chromosomes within the Lemna genus, with only a single translocation consistently identified specifically in L. turionifera. W. australiana has 20 chromosomes like S. polyrhiza, yet with significant architectural differences. In the Birchler Lab, antibodies against centromeric histone H3 were raised for four species to directly determine centromere organization and identify centromeric repeat sequences in Lemna species for the first time, revealing divergent centromere architecture in L. minor and L. turionifera that persists in their hybrids. All single chromosome sets of the sequenced species encode about 20,000 genes, significantly fewer than terrestrial monocots such as rice and Brachypodium, and comparable to the algae Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Methylome and small RNA sequencing revealed dramatic differences between the three genera and in contrast to model species, consistent with gene losses in known pathways of RNA directed DNA methylation. Analysis of missing and diverged orthogroups across the Lemnaceae, 10 other monocots and 7 non-monocots uncovered variations that likely account for these and other traits including: reduced morphology, aquatic habitat, clonal reproduction, dormancy, high photosynthetic rate, and lipid production (Ernst et al. 2025). Several studies have already utilized the novel genome references, which were made available before publication. In one example supported by this award, the Lam lab and collaborators conducted a single-cell transcriptomics study in Wolffia australiana, characterizing distinct tissue and cell types, and describing cell-type specific variations in circadian gene expression (Denyer et al. 2024). Follow-on experiments in the Lam lab confirmed that natural genetic variation in S. polyrhiza leads to variable turion production. RNA-sequencing of two genotypes at the extremes of turion yield identified turion-specific genes associated with dormancy, starch biosynthesis, and putative transcription factors that may be involved in the developmental transition. In addition, turion-specific expression of genes involved in lipid metabolism and oil biosynthesis were found in both S. polyrhiza as well as L. turionifera.
